beats.headline: GHOST ATTACK?
beats.short_title: The Gulf of Tonkin Attack That Never Happened 🔍 Case #11
beats.comment: Were the boats really there? 🚤 yes / 👻 no
beats.bonus: On 2 August 1964 USS Maddox really fought North Vietnamese torpedo boats. On the stormy night of 4 August, Maddox and Turner Joy reported a second attack; the Maddox's commander soon cabled doubts about freak radar returns and overeager sonarmen. President Johnson went on TV that night, and on 7 August Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (House 416-0, Senate 88-2). A declassified NSA history released in 2005 concluded the 4 August attack never happened.
beats.caption: The second Gulf of Tonkin attack never happened, and the NSA admitted it in 2005.

A relief ship reached a lonely lighthouse after Christmas, and nobody came down to meet it.
beats.headline: THE KEEPERS VANISHED?
beats.short_title: Three Lighthouse Keepers Vanished in 1900 🔦 Case #13
beats.comment: What do you think happened? 👻 taken / 🌊 the sea
beats.bonus: On 26 December 1900 the relief ship Hesperus reached the Flannan Isles lighthouse in Scotland's Outer Hebrides; a passing steamer had reported the light out on 15 December. All three keepers were gone, the clocks had stopped and one keeper's oilskin coat still hung inside. Damage at the west landing led the official inquiry to conclude they were most likely swept away by a huge wave. The 'uneaten meal' and 'overturned chair' come from Wilfrid Gibson's 1912 poem 'Flannan Isle'.
beats.caption: Three lighthouse keepers vanished in 1900. Meatball opened the file.

Soviet drillers pushed a drill seven miles into the Earth, and a story says the hole started screaming.

shots.photo: Soviet stamp of the Kola Superdeep Borehole (1987)

beats.headline: SCREAMS FROM HELL?
beats.short_title: The 'Well to Hell': Did Scientists Hear Screams? 🔥 Case #18
beats.comment: Would you listen down the hole? 👂 yes / 🙉 no way
beats.bonus: The Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, started in 1970, reached 12,262 metres (about 7.6 miles) in 1989, the deepest hole ever drilled, only about 23 cm wide. Drilling stopped when rock temperatures hit about 180 °C, and the hole is now welded shut under a metal cap. The 'screams from hell' story spread through broadcasts and newsletters in 1989-90 and has no source in the project's records.
beats.caption: The deepest hole on Earth and the 'Well to Hell' legend.

Three schoolgirls started laughing in class, and hours later they still couldn't stop.
beats.headline: A LAUGHING PLAGUE?
beats.short_title: The 1962 Laughter Epidemic Was REAL 😂 Case #20
beats.comment: Could this happen today? 😬 yes / 🙅 no way
beats.bonus: The Tanganyika laughter epidemic began on 30 January 1962 at a girls' boarding school in Kashasha, near Lake Victoria in what is now Tanzania. It started with three girls and affected 95 of the 159 pupils; the school closed in March. It spread to villages and other schools, about 1,000 people in all, and 14 schools shut before it died out about 18 months later. Researchers class it as mass psychogenic illness (mass hysteria), not an infection.
beats.caption: In 1962 a laughing outbreak closed 14 schools.
sources: Wikipedia, Tanganyika laughter epidemic: began 30 Jan 1962 at a mission boarding school for girls in Kashasha; started with three girls, 95 of 159 pupils affected; school closed 18 March 1962; spread to nearby villages; about 1,000 people affected and 14 schools shut; symptoms included crying, fainting and breathing problems; ended about 18 months after it began; classed as mass psychogenic illness; stress after independence (Dec 1961) suggested — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_laughter_epidemic (checked 2026-10-26)
Hempelmann, C. F., 'The laughter of the 1962 Tanganyika laughter epidemic', Humor 20(1), 2007

beats.say: A virus, or the mind? Guess.

It wasn't funny for long. It shut down a whole region's schools. Here's how.
See, in January 1962, at a girls' boarding school near Lake Victoria, three students started laughing.
Then their friends did. Within weeks, ninety-five of the school's girls had it.
Laughing and crying fits that came and went for hours, sometimes days.
Guess one: something in the water. Doctors tested. Nothing.
Guess two: a really, really good joke. I wish. No joke.
I tried to stay serious for this case. I lasted four seconds.
Wait. Here's the thing. When the school closed, the girls went home, and it spread.
Verdict: real. Doctors call it mass hysteria, a stress reaction that spreads between people, not a germ.
About a thousand people. Fourteen schools closed.
The country had just become independent. Researchers think stress was the spark.
Then, about eighteen months after it began, it simply faded away.
Nobody was seriously hurt. But nobody has forgotten it.
The only epidemic in history where the cure was closing school.
